headline: The deadlock ends here.
intro: You need experience to get hired. You need to be hired to get experience. That's the trap, and it's fake. Below are 32 real, self-contained jobs you can start right now, with no client and no permission. Each one produces a real deliverable: a reconciled set of books, a working automation, a finished video, a rebuilt calendar. Finish one, and you have proof in hand.
creed: You don't need permission to do the work. No client, no problem, do the job anyway and the artifact IS your experience. Nobody asks whether you were paid for it; they ask whether you can do it. Nothing happens if you do nothing. Start with one.

tasks.title: Rescue a Founder's Inbox From Chaos
tasks.proves: You can build an inbox system that turns email chaos into a same-day response standard, the #1 thing founders hire executive ops for.

prerequisites.skill: Gmail labels, filters, and search operators
prerequisites.why: The whole triage system runs on labels + filters, if you can't nest labels or write a filter rule, you can't build it.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: Google's own Gmail Filters & Labels help center (open), 20 minutes, hands-on.

prerequisites.skill: A basic inbox triage decision framework (e.g. the 4 D's: Do, Delegate, Defer, Delete)
prerequisites.why: You need a decision rule for every email, not just folders to dump them in.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: DevUp's /method, the UNSTICK and FIND methods teach the same decision-first thinking.

resources.name: Enron Email Dataset (Kaggle)
resources.what: A no-cost, public, real corporate inbox (500k+ emails), pull a 50-email sample to stand in for your 'client's' inbox.

resources.name: Gmail Filters & Labels
resources.what: Official how-to for building the label taxonomy and auto-filters you'll design.

resources.name: Google Workspace Learning Center
resources.what: Fast primer on Gmail power-user features (search operators, multiple inboxes).

brief.scenario: Mara Dizon runs a 3-person SaaS startup solo. She hasn't opened her inbox in nine days, 400+ unread, real client requests buried under cold pitches and newsletters. She's about to miss a contract renewal because of it.
brief.deliverable: A 6-label triage taxonomy, a written triage SOP (the decision rule for every incoming email), and a worked example: 50 real emails from the Enron dataset sorted into your taxonomy with a one-line reason for each.
constraints: Maximum 6 labels, more than that isn't a system, it's a new mess.
Every label needs a plain-English rule for what goes in it.
Must include a stated response-time promise per label (e.g. 'Client, same business day').
steps: Download a 50–100 email sample from the Enron dataset.
Read all of them once, tallying what categories naturally emerge.
Design a 6-label taxonomy with a one-sentence rule per label.
Sort all 50 emails into your taxonomy, noting the reason for each call.
Write the triage SOP: how a new email gets labeled, when it gets answered, what gets auto-archived.
Write a 5-line 'inbox zero in 20 minutes' daily routine Mara can run herself.

definitionOfDone: Every one of the 50 sample emails has exactly one label.
Each label has a written rule a stranger could apply consistently.
The SOP names a response-time commitment for at least 3 of the labels.
A follow-up filter/search-operator query is written for at least 2 labels.
selfCritique: Could someone who's never met Mara sort her next 50 emails using only my SOP?
Did I create categories for how the emails clustered, or force them into a template?
Is any label vague enough that two people would file the same email differently?
tasks.presentIt: Present as a before/after: 'Inbox at 400+ unread, 9 days stale → sorted, labeled, SOP in place in 3 hours.' Screenshot the label sidebar and lead with the response-time promise, not the label names.
tasks.stretch: Build the actual Gmail filter rules (not just the taxonomy) using search operators, and write a 30-day audit checklist for keeping the inbox at zero.

tasks.title: Rebuild an Overbooked Executive's Calendar
tasks.proves: You can turn a reactive, back-to-back calendar into a protected, priority-driven schedule, the exact skill that gets you promoted to Chief of Staff.

prerequisites.skill: Google Calendar (recurring events, color-coding, multiple calendars)
prerequisites.why: The rebuild lives entirely in Calendar, you need to move fast in it.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: Google Calendar Help Center's 'Get started' guide (open).

prerequisites.skill: Time-blocking and priority frameworks (Eisenhower matrix or similar)
prerequisites.why: You can't decide what to protect without a framework for what matters.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: DevUp's Executive Operations track under /niches, or any no-cost Eisenhower Matrix explainer.

resources.name: Google Calendar
resources.what: Build the actual before/after calendar mockup here (a no-cost personal Google account works).

resources.name: Google Calendar Help Center
resources.what: Recurring events, working hours, and focus-time features you'll use in the rebuild.

resources.name: Eisenhower Matrix, no-cost explainer
resources.what: The urgent/important framework you'll use to decide what gets protected first.

brief.scenario: Dan Reyes is regional director at a mid-size logistics company. His calendar has 11–14 meetings a day, back-to-back, zero focus time, and three standing meetings nobody can explain the purpose of anymore.
brief.deliverable: An audit scoring one invented sample week (you build it) against 5 red flags, plus a rebuilt version of that week in a real Google Calendar showing protected focus blocks, a meeting-free morning, and a trimmed recurring-meeting list.
constraints: The rebuilt week must include at least 2 protected 90-minute focus blocks.
At least 2 of the original recurring meetings must be cut, shortened, or converted to async.
Every kept meeting needs a one-line stated purpose.
steps: Construct the messy 'before' week: 12+ meetings across 5 days, mixed durations, no gaps (this is your practice raw material).
Audit it against 5 red flags: no purpose stated, no prep time, back-to-back with no buffer, recurring with unclear owner, wrong attendee count.
Decide which meetings to cut, shorten, delegate, or convert to async, write the reason for each.
Build the 'after' week in a real Google Calendar with color-coded categories and protected focus blocks.
Write a one-page 'calendar policy' Dan can hand to his team (buffer rules, no-meeting mornings, decline criteria).

definitionOfDone: Before and after week are both viewable (screenshots or shared calendar link).
Every cut or changed meeting has a documented reason.
The after week includes real protected focus time, not just fewer meetings.
The calendar policy doc is one page and usable by someone else.
selfCritique: Would Dan agree to every cut, or did I remove things without a real reason?
Did I protect focus time in the highest-energy part of the day, or just wherever there was a gap?
Is the policy doc specific enough to prevent the calendar from drifting back to chaos in a month?
tasks.presentIt: Lead with the number: 'Cut a 14-meeting day to 8, added 3 hours of protected focus time per week.' Show the before/after calendar screenshots side by side.
tasks.stretch: Add a delegation matrix: for every cut meeting, name who could attend instead and draft the handoff message.

tasks.title: Reconcile Three Months of Messy Transactions
tasks.proves: You can take an unreconciled set of books and bring them current and audit-ready, the single skill that makes bookkeepers indispensable to a client.

prerequisites.skill: Double-entry bookkeeping basics (debits, credits, chart of accounts)
prerequisites.why: Reconciliation is meaningless if you don't understand what a transaction should hit.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: Intuit's no-cost QuickBooks Online Certification course covers this from zero.

prerequisites.skill: Bank reconciliation workflow inside QuickBooks Online or Xero
prerequisites.why: You need to run the reconciliation tool, not just understand the theory.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: QuickBooks Online's own trial plus its in-app guided tour.

resources.name: QuickBooks Online Certification
resources.what: Official Intuit training, covers chart of accounts, reconciliation, and reporting.

resources.name: QuickBooks Online trial
resources.what: 30-day trial (check the current trial length and limits before you start), do the actual reconciliation work inside the real tool, not a spreadsheet mockup.

resources.name: Kaggle sample bank transaction datasets
resources.what: Public sample transaction CSVs you can import as your practice client's messy bank feed.

brief.scenario: Riverside Coffee Roasters (a fictional 2-location café) hasn't reconciled its books since a bookkeeper quit three months ago. Owner transactions, duplicate vendor entries, and uncategorized deposits are piling up.
brief.deliverable: A QuickBooks Online (trial) company file with 3 months of sample transactions imported, fully reconciled, chart of accounts cleaned up, and a one-page cleanup report documenting every issue you found and fixed.
constraints: Every transaction must be categorized, nothing left in 'Uncategorized.'
Any duplicate must be identified and flagged, not silently deleted.
The reconciliation must tie the ending bank balance to the statement balance exactly.
steps: Set up a no-cost QuickBooks Online trial and create a practice company.
Import or manually enter ~60–100 sample transactions across 3 months (use a public sample dataset or build a realistic mix of sales, COGS, payroll, and owner draws).
Build/clean the chart of accounts to fit a small café business.
Categorize every transaction, flagging anything ambiguous.
Run the bank reconciliation for each of the 3 months until it ties out.
Write a cleanup report: what was wrong, what you fixed, what the owner should watch for going forward.

definitionOfDone: All 3 months show 'Reconciled' status with zero variance.
Zero transactions remain in an uncategorized or ask-my-accountant bucket.
The cleanup report lists at least 5 specific issues found and how each was resolved.
A basic P&L for the period can be generated without errors.
selfCritique: If the owner asked me to explain any single categorization, could I defend it?
Did I investigate ambiguous transactions, or guess and move on?
Does my cleanup report read like real findings, or like generic bookkeeping advice?
tasks.presentIt: Lead with the before/after: '3 months, 0% reconciled → 100% reconciled, audit-ready in under a week.' Screenshot the reconciliation summary screen, it's the single most convincing proof in bookkeeping.
tasks.stretch: Add a recurring-transaction rule set (bank rules) that would auto-categorize 80% of future transactions without manual work.

tasks.title: Build an Accounts Receivable Aging Cleanup
tasks.proves: You can turn a wall of overdue invoices into a prioritized collection plan, the difference between a bookkeeper and a bookkeeper who actually protects cash flow.

prerequisites.skill: Accounts receivable basics (invoice, aging buckets, days sales outstanding)
prerequisites.why: You need to know what 30/60/90-day buckets mean before you can triage them.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: Xero's no-cost 'Accounts Receivable 101' help articles.

prerequisites.skill: Spreadsheet formulas (SUMIF, conditional formatting)
prerequisites.why: The aging report and prioritization live in a spreadsheet you build yourself.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: DevUp's tracker-building lab at /build teaches the exact schema pattern you need.

resources.name: Xero Advisor Certification
resources.what: Covers AR workflows and aging reports inside Xero.

resources.name: Google Sheets
resources.what: Build the aging tracker and collection-priority sheet here.

resources.name: SCORE no-cost templates library
resources.what: Reference real invoice/AR terminology used by small businesses (study only, don't copy).

brief.scenario: Bright Path Tutoring (a fictional small tutoring agency, 30 active family clients) has $18,400 in unpaid invoices, some over 90 days old, and no idea which ones are at risk of never getting paid.
brief.deliverable: An AR aging spreadsheet (30 invented but realistic invoices) with 30/60/90+ day buckets, a risk score per client, and a written collection plan with a specific message template for each aging bucket.
constraints: Every invoice needs an aging bucket calculated by formula, not typed in by hand.
The oldest 20% of balances must have an individual follow-up plan, not a generic template.
Collection messages must escalate in tone/urgency by bucket, 30-day and 90-day can't read the same.
steps: Build 30 realistic invoice records: client name, invoice date, amount, due date.
Add a formula-driven aging bucket column (Current / 30 / 60 / 90+).
Add conditional formatting so overdue severity is visible at a glance.
Calculate total dollars at risk per bucket and total days sales outstanding.
Write 3 escalating collection message templates (friendly reminder, firm follow-up, final notice).
Build a short collection plan prioritizing the highest-dollar, oldest-aging accounts first.

definitionOfDone: Aging buckets are 100% formula-driven, not manually assigned.
Total dollars at risk is calculated and correctly summed per bucket.
All 3 escalation message templates exist and are meaningfully different in tone.
The top 5 highest-risk accounts have a specific, individual next action noted.
selfCritique: If a client asked why I prioritized one overdue account over another, do I have a real reason?
Would the 90-day message get me paid, or does it read as passive as the 30-day one?
Did I build a formula that recalculates automatically if I change today's date?
tasks.presentIt: Lead with the dollar figure: '$18,400 in receivables triaged into a prioritized 3-week collection plan.' Show the aging summary table as the hero visual, clients respond to the number.
tasks.stretch: Add a DSO (days sales outstanding) trend chart and a proposed late-payment policy (deposit requirements, interest terms) so the backlog doesn't recur.

tasks.title: Audit a Startup's Spending for Waste
tasks.proves: You can read raw expense data and surface real savings, proof you think like a financial partner, not just a data-entry clerk.

prerequisites.skill: Reading a P&L / expense report and recognizing common waste categories (duplicate subscriptions, unused seats, category creep)
prerequisites.why: The whole audit is pattern recognition across real spend categories.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: DevUp's /method FIND drill, plus any no-cost 'startup burn rate' explainer.

prerequisites.skill: Basic spreadsheet pivot tables or SUMIF grouping
prerequisites.why: You need to group and total expenses by vendor/category to spot the waste.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: Google Sheets' own no-cost pivot table tutorial in the Help Center.

resources.name: Google Sheets
resources.what: Build the expense audit and pivot summary here.

resources.name: Public SaaS spend benchmark reports
resources.what: No-cost published benchmarks on typical SaaS spend per employee, use to judge if a line item looks high.

resources.name: Public startup expense/burn breakdowns (Indie Hackers, r/SaaS threads)
resources.what: Real founders sharing real expense breakdowns, study the categories, not the numbers.

brief.scenario: Loopline (a fictional 12-person B2B SaaS startup) is burning faster than expected. The founder exports a year of expense data and asks: 'Where is this actually going, and what can we cut without hurting the team?'
brief.deliverable: A 12-month expense audit (build ~80 realistic line items yourself: software subscriptions, contractor payments, ads, travel) grouped by category, with the top 10 waste candidates flagged and a specific dollar-amount savings recommendation for each.
constraints: Every flagged item needs a stated reason (duplicate tool, unused seats, better alternative, wrong plan tier).
Recommendations must total to a specific annual savings number, not a vague estimate.
At least 3 flagged items must be software/SaaS spend, the most common startup leak.
steps: Build ~80 realistic expense line items across 12 months and 6–8 categories.
Group and total spend by category and by vendor using pivot tables.
Identify duplicate or overlapping tools (e.g. two project management apps).
Flag the top 10 waste candidates with a one-line reason each.
Calculate the total annual savings if all 10 recommendations were implemented.
Write a one-page summary memo for the founder, ranked by savings size.

definitionOfDone: Pivot table correctly totals spend by category and by vendor.
10 waste items are flagged, each with a specific dollar impact and reason.
Total savings figure is calculated, not estimated by eyeballing.
The memo is ranked biggest-savings-first, not in the order you found them.
selfCritique: Is every flagged item a real waste pattern, or did I pad the list to hit 10?
Would cutting my top recommendation hurt the team's ability to work?
Did I total the savings correctly, or is the headline number inflated?
tasks.presentIt: Lead with the annual savings figure in bold: 'Found $14,200/year in recoverable spend across 10 line items.' The pivot table screenshot plus the ranked memo is the whole portfolio piece.
tasks.stretch: Add a spend policy, approval thresholds and a quarterly subscription-audit cadence, so the waste doesn't come back.

tasks.title: Audit a Real Public Brand's Social Presence
tasks.proves: You can diagnose why a brand's social isn't working using only public data, the exact research skill clients pay a social media manager to have.

prerequisites.skill: Reading engagement signals (likes/comments/shares relative to follower count, not absolute numbers)
prerequisites.why: A brand with 500k followers and 40 likes per post is doing worse than one with 5k followers and 300 likes, the ratio is what matters, not the raw count.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: Meta's no-cost Social Media Marketing course covers engagement-rate basics.

prerequisites.skill: Content calendar structure (pillars, cadence, format mix)
prerequisites.why: The audit ends in a calendar recommendation, you need the shape of one first.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: DevUp's /build portfolio lab or Canva's no-cost content calendar course.

resources.name: Meta Social Media Marketing
resources.what: Official Meta training on content strategy and engagement metrics.

resources.name: Any real public brand's Instagram/TikTok/LinkedIn (your choice)
resources.what: Your actual audit subject, no login needed, just their public posts from the last 30 days.

resources.name: Canva Design Essentials
resources.what: You'll need this to actually design the 3 finished posts for the deliverable.

brief.scenario: Pick one real, public local or regional brand (a café, gym, boutique, or small e-commerce shop) with an active but under-performing social account, you're auditing it cold, from public posts alone, the same way you would for a prospective client.
brief.deliverable: A written audit (posting cadence, format mix, engagement-rate calculation, tone consistency, bio/link-in-bio effectiveness) plus a 30-day content calendar and 3 fully finished posts (real graphics in Canva, real captions) that fix the biggest gap you found.
constraints: Audit must cover their last 15+ posts minimum, not a cherry-picked sample.
You must calculate an actual engagement rate, not describe it qualitatively.
The 3 finished posts must be publish-ready, full caption, hashtag set, and a real designed graphic.
steps: Choose a real, public brand's account and log their last 15–20 posts.
Calculate engagement rate per post and average it; note posting cadence and format mix (photo/video/carousel).
Identify the single biggest gap (inconsistent posting, weak captions, no video, unclear bio, no CTA).
Design a 30-day content calendar with 3 content pillars addressing that gap.
Design and write 3 fully finished posts in Canva that demonstrate the fix.
Write a one-page audit summary a business owner could read in 3 minutes.

definitionOfDone: Engagement rate is calculated with a shown formula, not just stated as a number.
The single biggest gap is named specifically, backed by evidence from the post data.
30-day calendar has clear pillars and a stated cadence (e.g. 4x/week).
All 3 finished posts are complete, graphic, caption, hashtags, ready to publish.
selfCritique: Would this brand's actual owner recognize the gap I identified as their real problem?
Do my 3 sample posts sound like this brand's voice, or like generic social media copy?
Did I calculate engagement rate correctly (engagement ÷ followers, not ÷ posts)?
tasks.presentIt: Present as a case study: brand name, before engagement rate, the gap you found, and your 3 finished posts as visual proof. Never claim you worked for the brand, label it clearly as an unsolicited audit/practice project.
tasks.stretch: Turn the audit into a cold outreach message pitching the brand owner directly, using the application-message lab's 4-part structure.

tasks.title: Build a Repeatable 30-Day Content Calendar System
tasks.proves: You can design a content system that survives past day one, pillars, cadence, and a repeatable production process, not just a list of post ideas.

prerequisites.skill: Content pillar strategy (3–5 recurring themes that support a brand's goals)
prerequisites.why: A calendar without pillars is just a list of random ideas that runs out in two weeks.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: HubSpot's no-cost content strategy course covers pillar-based planning.

prerequisites.skill: Spreadsheet-based tracker design
prerequisites.why: The calendar itself is a tracker, status, dates, and an owner column.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: DevUp's /build 'Build Your Own Tracker' lab teaches the exact schema.

resources.name: HubSpot Content Marketing Certification
resources.what: Covers pillar strategy, cadence planning, and repurposing content across formats.

resources.name: Google Sheets
resources.what: Build the actual 30-day calendar tracker here, status column, dates, format, caption draft.

resources.name: Buffer's no-cost content calendar guide
resources.what: Real-world cadence benchmarks by platform (how often to post on IG vs TikTok vs LinkedIn).

brief.scenario: Coastal Grind (a fictional independent coffee roastery, one location, growing wholesale side) wants a consistent social presence but has posted only 4 times in the last 2 months, with no plan.
brief.deliverable: A 30-day content calendar spreadsheet with 4 content pillars, a stated posting cadence per platform, and every single day's post pre-planned with format, hook idea, and caption draft, plus 3 of those days fully designed and written as finished posts.
constraints: Exactly 4 content pillars, each tied to a specific business goal (e.g. wholesale leads, in-store foot traffic, brand story, product education).
Every calendar row needs a format (photo/video/carousel/reel), not just a topic.
The tracker must have a status column (Idea / Drafted / Scheduled / Posted) using data validation, per the tracker-lab pattern.
steps: Define 4 content pillars mapped to Coastal Grind's actual business goals.
Build the 30-day calendar spreadsheet: date, pillar, format, hook, caption draft, status.
Fill in all 30 days with real, specific ideas, no placeholder 'post something' rows.
Apply data validation to the status column and conditional formatting for overdue/unposted days.
Fully design and write 3 representative days as finished, publish-ready posts.
Write a short 'how to keep this alive' note: who updates it, how often, what happens when an idea runs dry.

definitionOfDone: All 30 days are filled with distinct, specific content ideas, no repeats, no filler.
Every pillar appears roughly evenly across the 30 days, not lopsided.
Status column uses a real dropdown (data validation), not free text.
3 finished posts exist as real deliverables, not just calendar rows.
selfCritique: If I deleted the pillar labels, could someone still tell which pillar each post belongs to?
Is this calendar something a real business could execute, or is it aspirational fluff?
Did I vary the format enough, or is it 30 days of static photos?
tasks.presentIt: Show the full calendar as a scrollable screenshot alongside the 3 finished posts. Lead with the system, not the ideas: 'Built a 30-day content engine with 4 pillars and a self-sustaining production tracker.'
tasks.stretch: Add a repurposing map showing how each pillar's content can be cut into 3 different formats (a Reel becomes a carousel becomes a caption-only post) to triple output without new ideas.

tasks.title: Produce a 3-Part Short-Form Video Series for a Public Product
tasks.proves: You can plan, shoot, and edit short-form video that follows a proven hook-retention-CTA structure, one of the highest-leverage, highest-paying skills in social media right now.

prerequisites.skill: Short-form video structure (hook in first 2 seconds, retention pacing, clear CTA)
prerequisites.why: Random footage with music isn't a strategy, the structure is what makes it convert.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: CapCut's own no-cost tutorials cover hook, pacing, and CTA structure.

prerequisites.skill: Basic phone-shot video (framing, lighting, stable shots) and CapCut editing
prerequisites.why: You're producing real finished video, not a storyboard, you need the actual production skill.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: CapCut's in-app tutorials (open) walk through cuts, captions, and pacing.

resources.name: CapCut
resources.what: No-cost mobile/desktop editor, shoot and edit all 3 videos here.

resources.name: TikTok Creative Center (public, no-cost)
resources.what: Real published top-performing ad and organic examples by category, study structure, don't copy content.

resources.name: CapCut official tutorials
resources.what: CapCut's own no-cost walkthroughs of short-form editing fundamentals, from the maker of the tool.

brief.scenario: You're building a UGC-style (user-generated-content style) video series for a real product you personally own or can access at no cost (a phone app, a drugstore skincare item, a snack, a public library service), treat it like a real brand deal even though nobody asked you to.
brief.deliverable: 3 finished short-form videos (15–45 seconds each, vertical, captioned) following a hook → problem → demo → CTA structure, each targeting a different angle on the same product (e.g. a pain-point angle, a comparison angle, a 'day in the life' angle).
constraints: Each video must hook within the first 2 seconds, no slow intros.
All 3 videos must have burned-in captions (accessibility + muted-autoplay reality).
Each video needs a distinct angle, 3 versions of the same script don't count.
steps: Pick a real, accessible product and study 5 real public examples of similar UGC-style content for structure.
Write 3 short scripts, each with a different angle, using a hook/problem/demo/CTA outline.
Shoot raw footage for all 3 (phone camera is fine, natural light, stable frame).
Edit each in CapCut: cuts on beat, captions burned in, background audio at appropriate level.
Export all 3 in vertical 9:16 format, ready to publish.
Write a one-line strategic rationale for each video's angle.

definitionOfDone: All 3 videos are fully edited, captioned, and exported, not scripts or storyboards.
Each hooks within 2 seconds (test by watching only the first 2 seconds, does it make sense to keep watching?).
Captions are accurate and burned in, not relying on platform auto-captions.
Each video has a clearly different angle from the other two.
selfCritique: Would I stop scrolling in the first 2 seconds if this appeared in my own feed?
Is the CTA clear, or does the video just end?
Do the 3 videos feel different, or are they the same video with different words?
tasks.presentIt: Present as a mini case study: the product, the 3 angles chosen and why, the videos, and what you'd test next (a 4th angle, a different hook style). This is the single strongest portfolio piece for a video-focused social role.
tasks.stretch: Post all 3 publicly on a real account and track actual view/engagement data for 7 days, real performance data beats any mockup.

tasks.title: Rescue a Chaotic Agency Sprint Board
tasks.proves: You can take an unmanaged task list and turn it into a board that actually tells the team what to do next, the core job of a PM.

prerequisites.skill: Kanban/sprint basics (backlog, in-progress, review, done; WIP limits)
prerequisites.why: Without a structure, you're just moving cards around, not managing a sprint.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: Asana Academy's no-cost 'Kanban fundamentals' course.

prerequisites.skill: Writing a task/user story that a stranger could execute without asking questions
prerequisites.why: A board full of vague tasks ('fix the thing') is unmanageable no matter how it's organized.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: DevUp's SOP-building lab at /build teaches the same one-action-per-step discipline.

resources.name: Asana Academy
resources.what: Official Asana training on sprint boards, dependencies, and workload views.

resources.name: Asana / ClickUp / Trello no-cost tier
resources.what: Build the actual rescued board here (any of the three has a generous no-cost plan).

resources.name: Google Project Management Certificate (open to audit)
resources.what: Coursera lets you audit the full course no-cost, covers sprint planning and risk tracking.

brief.scenario: Halden Creative (a fictional 8-person design agency) runs client work through one giant unsorted task list, 60+ tasks, no owners on a third of them, no due dates, three tasks marked 'urgent' that have sat for a month.
brief.deliverable: A rebuilt sprint board (in Asana, ClickUp, or Trello no-cost tier) with 60 realistic tasks organized into a proper Kanban structure, clear columns, WIP limits, every task with an owner, due date, and client tag, plus a one-page 'how we run sprints now' SOP.
constraints: Every task must have an owner and a due date, no exceptions, even placeholder tasks.
WIP limit on the 'In Progress' column, enforced and explained.
At least 10 of the original 60 tasks must be identified as duplicates, stale, or no longer needed and explicitly archived (not silently deleted).
steps: Build the messy 'before' state: 60 realistic agency tasks across 4 client projects, deliberately disorganized (this is your practice raw material).
Audit the list: flag duplicates, stale tasks, and missing owners/dates.
Design the board structure: columns, WIP limits, tagging system by client.
Migrate and clean all 60 tasks into the new board with full metadata.
Archive (don't delete) the flagged duplicates/stale items with a note on why.
Write the one-page sprint SOP: how a task enters the board, how WIP limits are enforced, what 'done' means.

definitionOfDone: 100% of tasks on the new board have an owner and a due date.
WIP limit is set and would visibly block overloading a column.
At least 10 stale/duplicate tasks were found, archived, and logged with a reason.
The SOP defines a clear Definition of Done for at least one task type.
selfCritique: Could a new hire look at this board and know exactly what to work on next?
Did I reduce chaos, or just make the same chaos look tidier?
Is my WIP limit realistic for an 8-person team, or arbitrary?
tasks.presentIt: Lead with the before/after count: '60 unsorted tasks, 1/3 with no owner → fully triaged sprint board with WIP limits and a working SOP.' Screenshot both board states side by side.
tasks.stretch: Add a workload view showing each team member's current load, and flag anyone over-allocated relative to the others.

tasks.title: Build a Cross-Team Status Reporting Dashboard

prerequisites.ifYouDont: Canva Design Essentials (open).

brief.scenario: Pick one real, public video (yours if you have one, or a real public video you'd redesign as a practice exercise, never claim you made the actual video) and design 3 genuinely different thumbnail concepts testing 3 different psychological hooks (curiosity gap, big-number/stat callout, emotional face reaction).
brief.deliverable: 3 finished, export-ready thumbnail designs (1280x720) for the same video, each built around a distinct hook strategy, plus a written A/B test hypothesis for each ('I expect Concept B to outperform because...') and a small-size readability check screenshot for all 3.
constraints: All 3 thumbnails must be for the exact same video/topic, variation must come from strategy, not from designing 3 different videos.
Each thumbnail needs 5 words of text or fewer, YouTube's own design guidance, not a suggestion.
You must screenshot all 3 at simulated small size (like a mobile home feed) to prove readability.
steps: Choose a real public video/topic to redesign as practice.
Define 3 distinct hook strategies (curiosity gap, stat/number callout, emotional reaction).
Design thumbnail concept 1 at full 1280x720 resolution.
Design thumbnail concept 2 and concept 3, each genuinely different in composition, not just recolored.
Shrink all 3 down to simulate a mobile feed and screenshot the readability test.
Write a one-line testable hypothesis for each concept explaining why it might win.

definitionOfDone: All 3 thumbnails are exported at correct 1280x720 resolution.
Each uses a genuinely different composition/hook, not a palette-swap of the same layout.
Text is 5 words or fewer on every thumbnail.
All 3 pass the small-size readability check (legible and clear at simulated mobile size).
selfCritique: If I saw all 3 in a crowded YouTube feed at actual size, could I read the text and understand the hook in under 1 second?
Are the 3 concepts testing genuinely different hooks, or minor variations of the same idea?
Would my hypothesis for the 'winning' concept be falsifiable by real click-through data?
tasks.presentIt: Present all 3 side by side at both full size and simulated small size, with the hypothesis for each labeled clearly. Frame it as an A/B test plan, not just 'here are 3 thumbnails', the testing methodology is the actual skill being proven.
tasks.stretch: If you have access to a real channel (yours or with permission), run the test live and report real click-through-rate data after a few days.

tasks.title: Edit a 60-Second Product Explainer From Raw Screen Recordings

prerequisites.skill: Screen recording basics (a no-cost tool like OBS Studio or a built-in OS recorder)
prerequisites.why: You need real raw footage to edit, this task isn't about stock footage, it's about turning messy screen capture into something polished.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: OBS Studio's own no-cost getting-started guide, or your OS's built-in screen recorder (no install needed).

prerequisites.skill: Video editing fundamentals: cuts, pacing, text overlays, background music licensing
prerequisites.why: The explainer needs professional pacing and legally clean audio, not just raw footage with a voiceover.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: DevUp's CapCut Editing Masterclass, or CapCut/DaVinci Resolve's own no-cost tutorials.

resources.name: OBS Studio (no-cost, open source)
resources.what: Record raw screen footage of the no-cost tool you'll be explaining.

resources.what: Legally clean background music, never use unlicensed commercial tracks in client-style work.

brief.scenario: Pick one real, no-cost-tier SaaS or app tool you genuinely use or can access (a note app, a no-cost design tool, a habit tracker) and treat it as a client who needs a 60-second 'what is this and why should I care' explainer for their landing page.
brief.deliverable: A finished 60-second explainer video: raw screen recording of the tool's core feature, edited with a clear 3-act structure (problem → solution demo → CTA), text overlays for key points, licensed background music, and a written voiceover script (recorded yourself, or as on-screen text if you're not comfortable on mic).
constraints: Must be 60 seconds or under, explainer videos live or die on tightness, not completeness.
Must follow a problem → solution → CTA structure, explicitly identifiable in the edit.
Background music must be from a verifiably no-cost/licensed source, no exceptions.
steps: Choose a real no-cost tool and identify its single clearest core value proposition.
Write a tight script: what problem it solves (10–15 sec), how it works (30–35 sec), CTA (10–15 sec).
Record raw screen footage demonstrating the actual product flow, cleanly and deliberately.
Edit: cut down to the essential moments, add text overlays for key points, sync pacing to the script.
Add licensed background music at an appropriately low volume under any voiceover.
Export at a standard resolution (1080p) and do a final full watch-through for pacing issues.

definitionOfDone: Final video is 60 seconds or under, exported and playable.
The problem → solution → CTA structure is clearly identifiable when watching.
All footage is real screen recording of the actual tool, not stock footage or slides.
Music is confirmed royalty-free/licensed, and audio levels don't drown out any voiceover or overlay text.
selfCritique: Would someone unfamiliar with this tool understand what it does and why they'd want it after watching once?
Did I cut every dead moment, or does the pacing drag anywhere?
Is the CTA clear and specific, or does the video just fade out?
tasks.presentIt: Present as a mini case study: the tool, the core value prop you chose to lead with, and the finished video embedded/linked. Lead with the constraint you nailed: 'Turned raw, unscripted screen capture into a 58-second, problem-solution-CTA explainer.'
tasks.stretch: Cut a second, 15-second vertical version of the same explainer for social/story placements, proving you can adapt one asset across formats, a real recurring client need.

prerequisites.why: The whole setup lives in OBS scenes and sources, you have to build fluently in it, not just watch a tutorial.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: OBS Project's own no-cost Quickstart guide walks through scenes and sources in about 30 minutes.

prerequisites.skill: Basic overlay design in a no-cost tool like Canva

resources.what: Build the actual scene collection here, the whole deliverable is a working OBS setup, not a mockup.

resources.what: Official getting-started guide for scenes, sources, and scene collections.

resources.what: Design the starting-soon, BRB, and ending overlays here to one consistent look.

brief.scenario: Jio Ramos wants to stream his gameplay three nights a week, but every attempt dies in setup, no intro screen, audio that clips, and a desktop full of notifications on camera. He has the hardware; he just needs someone to make the software ready to go live.
brief.deliverable: A finished OBS scene collection (exported as a shareable file) with at least 5 scenes, Starting Soon, Live, Just Chatting, BRB, and Ending, each with the right sources wired up, plus 3 matching overlay graphics and a one-page 'how to go live' checklist Jio can follow without you.
constraints: At least 5 named, purpose-built scenes, a single scene you rename doesn't count as a setup.
Audio must have a noise gate or filter on the mic so it doesn't clip or pick up room hiss.
The 3 overlay frames must share one consistent visual style, not three random templates.
steps: Install OBS and create a new scene collection named for the streamer.
Build the 5 core scenes and wire each one's sources (display/game capture, camera, mic, overlays).
Design the 3 overlay frames in Canva to a single consistent style and import them.
Add an audio filter chain to the mic (noise suppression plus noise gate) and set levels so nothing clips.
Export the scene collection and record a short screen capture proving each scene switches cleanly.
Write the one-page 'go live in 5 minutes' checklist: what to open, what to check, in what order.

definitionOfDone: The scene collection has 5+ working scenes and can be exported as a file.
The mic has a real audio filter chain, and a test recording shows no clipping.
All 3 overlay frames share one consistent style (same fonts, colors, layout logic).
The go-live checklist is followable by the streamer with you not in the room.
selfCritique: Could Jio go live tonight using only my checklist, without messaging me once?
Does the audio actually sound clean on a test recording, or did I just assume the filter worked?
Do my three overlays look like one brand, or three free templates stuck together?
tasks.presentIt: Present as a short before/after screen recording: a blank OBS window becomes a full scene collection switching cleanly between Starting Soon, Live, and BRB. Lead with the outcome: 'A streamer who couldn't get online is now one click from live.'
tasks.stretch: Add a 'Live Selling' or 'Guest' scene with a two-camera layout, and set up hotkeys so scene switching is one keypress instead of a mouse hunt.

tasks.title: Cut a Long Stream Into a Week of Short-Form Clips
tasks.proves: You can mine a multi-hour stream for its best 30 seconds and turn one broadcast into a week of vertical clips, the repurposing engine most streamers need but few have time to run themselves.

prerequisites.skill: Short-form vertical editing in CapCut (cuts, captions, hooks)
prerequisites.why: The clips are real finished vertical videos, not timestamps, you need to actually cut and caption them.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: CapCut's own no-cost tutorials cover vertical cuts, captions, and pacing.

prerequisites.skill: Spotting a clippable moment (a hook, a payoff, a reaction)
prerequisites.why: Most of a stream is dead air; the skill is finding the 5 seconds worth reposting, not editing prettily.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: Study 10 top clips in TikTok's public Creative Center and note what happens in the first 2 seconds of each.

resources.name: A real public stream VOD (Twitch/YouTube, your choice)
resources.what: Your source footage, pick a public VOD you have the right to clip for practice, or record your own. Never repost someone's content as your own; label it a practice edit.

resources.what: No-cost editor, cut, caption, and export all clips vertically here.

brief.scenario: A streamer publishes 3–4 hour broadcasts and posts nothing else, so nobody who isn't already live ever finds them. One good stream is a week of content, it's just buried inside three hours of footage nobody will scrub through.
brief.deliverable: 5 finished vertical clips (15–40 seconds each, 9:16, captioned) pulled from a single long stream/VOD, each with a scroll-stopping first 2 seconds, plus a one-page clip log noting the source timestamp, the hook, and a suggested caption for each.
constraints: All 5 clips must come from ONE stream/VOD, the skill is mining one source, not editing five different videos.
Every clip needs burned-in captions, most short-form is watched on mute.
Each clip must stand alone, someone who never watched the stream should get it in the first 2 seconds.
steps: Pick one long public VOD (or your own recording) and scrub it, logging every potentially clippable moment with its timestamp.
Choose the 5 strongest moments, with a variety of hooks (funny, informative, high-skill, reaction).
Cut each to 15–40 seconds in CapCut, starting on the hook, not the wind-up.
Add accurate burned-in captions and a punchy on-screen title to each.
Export all 5 vertical (9:16) and do a mute-watch to confirm each reads without sound.
Write the clip log: source timestamp, the hook in one line, and a suggested caption for each clip.

definitionOfDone: All 5 clips are exported vertical, captioned, and 15–40 seconds long.
Every clip is pulled from the same single source stream.
Each clip makes sense in its first 2 seconds with the sound off.
The clip log ties each clip to its source timestamp and gives a ready-to-post caption.
selfCritique: Would I stop scrolling for each of these in my own feed, or only the best one or two?
Do the captions match the audio exactly, or did I let auto-captions ship with errors?
Did I pick 5 genuinely different moments, or 5 versions of the same beat?
tasks.presentIt: Present the 5 clips as a grid alongside the clip log. Lead with the leverage: 'One 3-hour stream became 5 ready-to-post vertical clips in an afternoon.' The clip log proves you have a repeatable process, not a lucky edit.
tasks.stretch: Post the clips on a real account across a week and track which hook type got the most watch-through, then write one line on what you'd cut more of next time.

tasks.title: Script and Staff a 60-Minute Live-Selling Show
tasks.proves: You can run the operations behind a live sale, a minute-by-minute run-of-show, a product rotation, and a chat-moderation plan, so the seller focuses on selling while you run the machine. This is the ops role live commerce is scrambling to hire.

prerequisites.skill: Live-selling format basics (product rotation, CTA cadence, urgency plays)
prerequisites.why: A live sale that just shows products at random doesn't convert, the structure and timing are the job.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: Watch 3 real TikTok/Facebook live sales end to end and note when and how they push the buy CTA.

prerequisites.skill: Chat moderation fundamentals (pinned messages, banned words, FAQ replies)
prerequisites.why: During a live sale, buying questions get buried in noise, the mod plan is what keeps orders from getting lost.

brief.scenario: Lea sells thrifted clothing on TikTok Live. Her streams ramble, she forgets to restate the price, loses track of who commented 'mine,' and never quite closes. She sells more in a chaotic hour than a calm one should have to, and she knows it.
brief.deliverable: A minute-by-minute run-of-show for a 60-minute live sale (segments, product rotation, CTA cadence), a product line-up sheet (10–12 invented but realistic items with prices and hero picks), and a one-page chat-moderation SOP covering pinned messages, claim handling, banned words, and canned FAQ replies.
constraints: The run-of-show must be timed to the minute, 'sell the jackets' isn't a plan; '0:12–0:18, jacket rotation, restate price every 90 seconds' is.
The CTA (how to buy / how to claim) must repeat on a stated cadence, not just once at the start.
The moderation SOP must define exactly how a buyer claims an item so no order is lost in the chat scroll.
steps: Study 3 real live sales end to end and note their segment structure and CTA timing.
Build the product line-up sheet: 10–12 items, prices, and which 2–3 are the hero draws.
Write the 60-minute run-of-show in timed blocks: intro hook, product rotations, mid-show recap, urgency close.
Set the CTA cadence, exactly when and how the how-to-buy message repeats.
Write the moderation SOP: pinned message, the claim rule, banned-words list, and 5 canned FAQ replies.
Add an 'if it goes wrong' note: what the mod does if orders pile up faster than they can be logged.

definitionOfDone: The run-of-show is timed to the minute for the full 60 minutes.
The CTA repeats on a clearly stated cadence, not once.
The moderation SOP defines an unambiguous claim rule a stranger could enforce.
The product sheet names the hero items and their prices, not just a list.
selfCritique: If I handed this to a mod who'd never seen the show, could they run chat without asking a question?
Does the run-of-show build urgency toward a close, or just list products in order?
Is my claim rule airtight, or could two buyers claim the same item and both think they won?
tasks.presentIt: Present the run-of-show, product sheet, and moderation SOP as one show kit. Lead with the operator angle: 'A repeatable 60-minute live-sale system the seller can run every week, script, line-up, and chat plan in one kit.'
tasks.stretch: Add a post-show pack: an order-reconciliation sheet that turns claims into a fulfillment list, plus a 3-clip repurposing plan for the best moments of the sale.

tasks.title: Edit a Raw Podcast Episode to Broadcast-Clean
tasks.proves: You can take a messy raw recording, filler words, dead air, uneven levels, and deliver a tight, clean episode a host would publish without a second listen. This is a core deliverable of most podcast retainers.

prerequisites.why: The whole job is hands-on editing, you need to actually cut, not just know the theory.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: Descript's no-cost tutorials and help center walk through filler removal and leveling.

prerequisites.why: A clean edit still sounds amateur if one voice is loud, the other quiet, and there's hiss underneath.

resources.name: A public-domain or Creative Commons recorded conversation (or your own)
resources.what: Your raw source, a CC-licensed interview, a public recording you may edit, or a 20-minute chat you record yourself. Keep it honest: don't pass off someone's show as your work.

resources.what: Edit the episode here (check the current free-tier limits before you start); text-based editing makes filler removal fast.

brief.scenario: A first-time host records a 25-minute conversation on his phone and a guest's laptop mic. It's full of filler, two false starts, a 40-second tangent about parking, and the guest is half the volume of the host. He loves the content and dreads the edit.
brief.deliverable: A finished, exported episode (target 15–20 minutes from the raw 25) that's been de-filled, tightened, level-matched, and noise-cleaned, with a simple intro and outro added, plus a short edit-decision log listing what you cut and why.
constraints: Filler words and dead air must be removed without making the conversation sound choppy or unnatural.
Both voices must sit at a consistent, matched loudness, no reaching for the volume knob between speakers.
The edit log must note at least one judgment call where you cut content, not just filler (a tangent, a repeat, a dead story).
steps: Import the raw recording and do one full listen, marking filler, dead air, and any tangent worth cutting.
Remove filler words and dead air, keeping the natural rhythm of speech.
Make the harder cuts, the tangent, the false start, and log each one.
Level-match the voices and run noise cleanup so both speakers sound consistent and clean.
Add a simple intro and outro (a title read and a sign-off; music optional and licensed).
Export the final episode and write the edit-decision log: total time cut, and the reasoning for each content cut.

definitionOfDone: The exported episode is noticeably tighter than the raw file with no choppy, unnatural cuts.
Both voices are level-matched and free of obvious background noise.
An intro and outro are present.
The edit log documents at least one content cut (beyond filler) with a reason.
selfCritique: Does the edit sound natural, or can you hear every cut?
Would the host notice the guest was originally half the volume, or is it seamless now?
Did I cut for the listener's time, or leave in a tangent because cutting felt risky?
tasks.presentIt: Present a 60-second before/after: 30 seconds of raw audio, 30 seconds of your edit, plus the edit log. Lead with the transformation: '25 minutes of raw phone audio became an 18-minute episode ready to publish.' The before/after clip is the whole proof.
tasks.stretch: Deliver a clips bonus: pull the single best 45-second exchange as a standalone audiogram with captions, the kind of add-on that turns a one-off edit into a retainer.

brief.scenario: A host publishes a solid weekly episode and then nothing. No show notes, no clips, no social. The episode goes up, a few loyal listeners hear it, and it disappears. One recording that could have fed a week of posts feeds none.
brief.deliverable: A complete repurposing pack for one episode: full show notes (a 2–3 sentence summary, 5–7 timestamped chapters, 3 key takeaways, and any links mentioned), 3 title/subject-line options, 2 designed quote cards, and a 3-clip pick list (timestamps plus suggested captions) ready for an editor to cut.
constraints: Timestamps must be real and accurate to the actual episode, not invented.
The 3 title options must be genuinely different angles, not one title reworded three ways.
The 2 quote cards must pull real, verbatim quotes from the episode and share one consistent visual style.
steps: Listen to the full episode once, noting timestamps for each topic shift and any strong quote.
Write the show notes: a tight summary, 5–7 timestamped chapters, and 3 key takeaways.
Collect any links or references mentioned and list them cleanly.
Write 3 title/subject-line options, each from a different angle (curiosity, benefit, guest name).
Design 2 quote cards in Canva from real quotes, in one consistent style.
Write the 3-clip pick list: timestamp, why it's clippable, and a suggested caption for each.

definitionOfDone: Show notes include a summary, 5–7 accurate timestamped chapters, and 3 takeaways.
All timestamps match the real episode.
3 distinct title options and 2 styled quote cards are complete.
The clip pick list gives an editor exact timestamps and captions to work from.
selfCritique: Could a listener decide whether to hit play using only my summary and chapters?
Are my 3 titles really different bets, or the same title with synonyms?
Did I pull quote-card lines that stand alone, or ones that need the whole episode for context?
tasks.presentIt: Present the pack as one tidy document plus the two quote cards. Lead with the multiplier: 'One episode became show notes, 3 titles, 2 quote cards, and 3 clip picks, a week of content from a single recording.'
tasks.stretch: Add a 5-email or 5-caption drip that releases the episode's takeaways across the week, so the one recording keeps resurfacing instead of dropping once.

Build the volunteer roster: every role, its owner/slot, arrival time, and responsibilities.
Build the supplies checklist with one named owner per item.
Write the 3 comms messages: the invite, the volunteer brief, and the day-before reminder.

definitionOfDone: The run-of-show covers setup through teardown in timed blocks.
Every volunteer role has an owner and an arrival time.
Every supply item has exactly one named owner.
The comms plan includes at least 3 messages timed to different moments.

Is every gap covered, setup, teardown, the awkward transitions, or just the main event?
Would a volunteer know exactly where to be and what to do from their line of the roster?

brief.deliverable: A reusable Mailchimp newsletter template with a consistent structure (header, a devotional/reflection, community and announcements, an event or offer, and a closing), plus 4 fully written weekly issues that drop into it, and a one-page style guide defining the tone, sections, and send cadence.

All 4 issues must be fully written, not outlines, real devotional text, real announcements.
The style guide must state a specific send cadence and a clear tone rule (what this newsletter would and wouldn't say).
steps: Study 3 real ministry or wellness newsletters and note their recurring section structure.
Build the reusable template in Mailchimp with a branded header and fixed sections.
Write issue 1 in full as the reference issue.
Write issues 2–4, each with a fresh devotional and real-feeling announcements, all in the same structure.
Design a consistent header graphic in Canva and apply it across all 4.
Write the one-page style guide: tone rules, section definitions, and the send cadence.

definitionOfDone: The Mailchimp template has a fixed, reusable section structure.
All 4 issues are fully written and drop cleanly into the template.
A consistent branded header appears across every issue.
The style guide states a specific cadence and a clear tone rule.
selfCritique: If I handed this to the coach, could they send issue 5 next week without me?
Do all 4 issues feel like one voice, or four different writers?
Is the devotional section genuinely reflective, or does it read like a marketing email in disguise?
tasks.presentIt: Present the template plus the 4 issues as a set, with the style guide up front. Lead with the consistency win: 'A newsletter system that turns an occasional, whenever-someone-remembers send into a dependable weekly rhythm.' Show the template structure as the hero, the system is the value, not any single issue.
tasks.stretch: Add a 3-email welcome sequence for new subscribers so people who join mid-month get a warm on-ramp before the weekly rhythm picks them up.

tasks.title: Turn One Sermon Into a Week of Social Content
tasks.proves: You can turn a single sermon or talk into a week of shareable clips and graphics, so a message reaches the people who weren't in the room. Repurposing is how small ministries grow without a media team, and the skill they hand to one trusted person.

prerequisites.skill: Short-form vertical clip editing (CapCut: cuts, captions)
prerequisites.why: The clips are real finished videos, you need to cut and caption, not just pick timestamps.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: CapCut's no-cost tutorials cover vertical cuts and captions.

prerequisites.skill: Quote-graphic design in Canva
prerequisites.why: The pack includes designed quote cards, not just video, you produce real graphics.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: Canva Design School's no-cost basics.

resources.name: One public sermon or wellness talk (your choice)
resources.what: Your source, a publicly posted sermon or talk you may clip for a practice piece. Label it unsolicited practice; never imply the ministry hired you.

resources.name: CapCut
resources.what: Cut and caption the vertical clips here.

resources.name: Canva (no-cost tier)
resources.what: Design the quote cards and captions here.

brief.scenario: A local pastor preaches a strong 35-minute message every Sunday to the same room, then posts the full video where almost no one watches past two minutes. Inside that one sermon are three moments that could reach thousands, if someone cut them out and gave them a life of their own.
brief.deliverable: A week's social pack from one sermon/talk: 3 finished vertical clips (20–45 seconds, captioned) built around one clear idea each, 3 quote graphics in Canva pulling verbatim lines, and a caption pack (a ready-to-post caption for each of the 6 pieces) with a simple posting schedule.
constraints: All content must come from ONE sermon/talk, the skill is mining one message fully.
Every clip needs burned-in captions and must make sense to someone who wasn't there.
The 3 quote graphics must use real verbatim lines and share one consistent visual style.
steps: Watch the full sermon/talk and log the 3 strongest self-contained moments with timestamps.
Cut each into a 20–45 second vertical clip in CapCut, starting on the idea, not the setup.
Add accurate burned-in captions to each clip.
Design 3 quote graphics in Canva from verbatim lines, in one consistent style.
Write a ready-to-post caption for each of the 6 pieces.
Lay it out on a simple 1-week posting schedule (which piece posts which day).

definitionOfDone: 3 captioned vertical clips and 3 styled quote graphics are complete, all from one source.
Every clip stands alone for someone who didn't hear the full message.
The quote graphics use verbatim lines and share one visual style.
A caption pack and a 1-week posting schedule tie the 6 pieces together.
selfCritique: Would each clip make a scroller stop, or do they only land if you already heard the sermon?
Are the captions accurate word-for-word, or did I ship auto-caption errors?
Did I honor the message's meaning, or clip it into something the pastor didn't say?
tasks.presentIt: Present the 6 pieces plus the schedule as a one-week content calendar. Lead with the reach angle: 'One 35-minute sermon became a week of clips and graphics that travel past the room it was preached in.' Always label it as a practice repurposing project, not commissioned work.
tasks.stretch: Add a short audiogram version of one clip for audio-first platforms, and write a one-line note on which of the three ideas you'd expect to travel furthest and why.

tasks.title: Deliver One Pro-Bono Project for a Real Organization
tasks.time: 1–2 weeks, a few hours per week
tasks.proves: You can scope, deliver, and hand over real work for a real stakeholder, with a named organization willing to vouch for it. This is the closest thing to client experience that requires no client.

prerequisites.skill: One deliverable you can already produce (from any other task on this page)
prerequisites.why: Pro-bono work is where you apply a skill for a real stakeholder, not where you learn it from zero. Bring one thing you can do.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: Finish one Starter micro-task above first: it gives you the exact deliverable to offer.

resources.name: Your own community
resources.what: A school, parish, barangay health center, co-op, or small local business: every one of them has a broken spreadsheet, an unmanaged page, or books nobody reconciles.

brief.scenario: Choose one real organization near you and offer one clearly-scoped piece of work, no-cost. Put your hours where they do the most good; a small org with no budget gains more from ten of your hours than a large one ever would, and effective help is targeted: one real problem, solved completely, handed over so they can keep it running without you.
brief.deliverable: The finished work itself, plus a one-page handover the org can use after you leave: what you built, how to maintain it, and where everything lives.
constraints: Scope it in writing before you start: one deliverable, one deadline, agreed with a named person. Pro-bono without scope becomes an unpaid job.
Treat it exactly like paid work: professional communication, deadlines kept, confidentiality respected. This is conduct practice as much as craft practice.
Deliver a handover document. Work that collapses when you leave helped nobody.
steps: List 3 organizations you already have a connection to, and for each, one visible problem you could fix.
Contact the most promising one with a specific offer: the problem, the deliverable, the deadline. Specific offers get yes; vague offers get silence.
Agree the scope in writing (a message thread counts). Then deliver it like a paid engagement.
Hand over: walk them through the work, leave the one-page guide, and ask one question: 'may I show this work, with your name, when I apply for jobs?'

definitionOfDone: The deliverable is live and in use by the organization, not just finished on your laptop.
A named person at the org has the handover document and can run things without you.
You have written permission to present the work publicly.
selfCritique: Did I scope this in writing before starting, or did the work grow past the agreement?
Could the org keep using what I built if I disappeared today?
Did I pick the org where my hours did the most good, or just the easiest ask?
tasks.presentIt: Present it as your first case study: the organization, the problem, the deliverable, and one real outcome. 'Rebuilt the enrollment sheet for a 40-student tutorial center; staff now update it themselves' beats any certificate on the page.
tasks.stretch: After handover, offer a second org the same deliverable. Two named organizations plus two handover docs is a portfolio, and a referral network you earned by giving first.

tasks.title: Turn a Doctor Visit Into a Clean SOAP Note
tasks.proves: You can chart a clinical visit accurately and catch an AI scribe's mistakes: the exact skill US practices now pay a medical VA a premium for.

prerequisites.skill: Core medical terminology (body systems, common abbreviations, drug/route basics)
prerequisites.why: You cannot chart what you can't read. A wrong term or misread abbreviation in a note is a clinical error, not a typo.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: Audit the University of Pittsburgh's Medical Terminology I on Coursera free: the first module covers enough to start.

prerequisites.skill: HIPAA basics (what PHI is, minimum-necessary, safe handling)
prerequisites.why: Every chart is protected health information. Handling it wrong is the fastest way to lose a medical client and expose them to a fine.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: Take a free HIPAA awareness course (HIPAA Journal lists several with certificates) before you touch any record.

resources.name: MTSamples
resources.what: Thousands of free, public sample medical transcriptions with no real patient PHI. Pick one visit report to chart from.

resources.name: Coursera: Medical Terminology I
resources.what: Audit free; the vocabulary you need to read and write the note.

resources.name: Freed AI scribe
resources.what: Free trial notes (one option among several AI scribes, Nabla is another; not an endorsement); generate an AI draft of the same visit to compare against your own.

brief.scenario: A US telehealth practice is drowning in unwritten notes. Their AI scribe drafts a SOAP note per visit, but a provider has to fix it before it's billable, and providers are the bottleneck. They want a VA who can chart cleanly and correct the AI so the provider only signs off. Prove you're that person.
brief.deliverable: One clean, structured SOAP note (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan) written by you from an MTSamples visit transcript, plus a short 'what the AI got wrong' list comparing your note to an AI-drafted version.
constraints: Use only MTSamples or synthetic data: never a real person's health information, even a friend's.
Every section (S/O/A/P) must be present and in clinician shorthand, not narrative paragraphs.
Flag anything the source is missing (no BP, no allergy check) rather than inventing it: a good scribe never fabricates a value.
steps: Pick one visit report from MTSamples (a general or family-practice note is easiest to start).
Write your own SOAP note from it: what the patient reports (S), measurable findings (O), the diagnosis/impression (A), and next steps (P).
Run the same transcript through Freed's free trial to get an AI-drafted note.
Compare the two line by line: list every place the AI added, dropped, or misstated something.
Write a two-line note on how you'd store and share this chart to stay HIPAA-compliant.

definitionOfDone: The SOAP note has all four sections, each in correct clinical shorthand and terminology.
No value is invented; anything missing from the source is flagged as missing.
The 'what the AI got wrong' list names at least two concrete differences with the correct fix.
A one-line HIPAA handling note explains how the chart is stored and who may see it.
selfCritique: Would a provider be able to sign this note as-is, or would they still have to rewrite it?
Did I catch the AI's errors, or did I trust its draft and miss a wrong term or dose?
Is there a single spot where I guessed a value instead of flagging it as absent?
tasks.presentIt: Present it as a before/after the way a clinic thinks: 'AI draft → provider still had to fix 4 things; my corrected note → sign-ready.' Redact nothing (there's no real PHI) and lead with the errors you caught: that list is the proof you're safe to hand a chart.
tasks.stretch: Chart three more MTSamples visits across different specialties (a mental-health intake, a dental note, a follow-up) and time yourself. A medical VA who charts a clean note in under 15 minutes is worth a retainer.

tasks.title: Model a Real Room and Render It Photorealistically
tasks.proves: You can take a flat floor plan, build an accurate 3D model, and produce a render a client could put in a listing: the core deliverable of every arch-viz and real-estate visualization gig.

prerequisites.skill: Basic 3D modeling in SketchUp or Blender (push/pull, components, materials)
prerequisites.why: The whole task is modeling to scale, then lighting it. If you can't extrude a wall or apply a material, you can't build the room.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: SketchUp Campus (open) or the Blender Guru beginner series on YouTube takes you from zero to a walled room in an afternoon.

prerequisites.skill: Reading a floor plan and its dimensions
prerequisites.why: A render is only worth anything if it's to scale. Misread the plan and every proportion is wrong.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: Any real-estate listing floor plan shows a scale and room dimensions. Practice reading three before you model one.

resources.name: SketchUp Free
resources.what: Free browser modeler: build the room to scale with no license.

resources.name: D5 Render
resources.what: Free Community tier with real-time ray tracing: light and render the model.

resources.name: A public floor plan
resources.what: Pull a real 2D floor plan from any real-estate listing to stand in for your 'client's' brief: no invented layouts.

brief.scenario: A real-estate agent is selling a unit that's still under construction. There are no photos, only a 2D floor plan. She needs one interior render and one key view to put on the listing so buyers can picture the space. All you get is the plan.
brief.deliverable: An accurate, to-scale 3D model of the unit, plus one photorealistic interior render and one key exterior or perspective view, sized for a listing.
constraints: Model to scale from the plan's real dimensions; never eyeball or invent a measurement.
Use believable real-world materials and lighting, not default grey boxes.
If the plan doesn't specify something (ceiling height, a finish), note your assumption rather than guessing silently: a good visualizer flags, doesn't fabricate.
steps: Pick one real-estate floor plan with visible dimensions to use as your brief.
Model the unit to scale in SketchUp Free: walls, openings, and the main fixtures.
Apply real materials (floor, walls, key furniture) and set up a natural light source.
Bring the model into D5 Render, stage one interior view, and render it photorealistically.
Render one key exterior or wide perspective, then write a two-line note listing every assumption you made where the plan was silent.

definitionOfDone: The model's room dimensions match the source floor plan (spot-check three walls).
Both renders use real materials and lighting, not default placeholders.
Every assumption made beyond the plan is written down, not hidden.
The two final images are exported at listing-ready resolution.
selfCritique: If the agent measured a wall against my model, would it match the plan?
Does this look like a real space a buyer could stand in, or like an untextured 3D exercise?
Did I invent any dimension or finish instead of flagging it as an assumption?
tasks.presentIt: Present it as the agent's problem solved: 'From a flat 2D plan to a listing-ready render.' Put the source floor plan and your final render side by side: the jump from line drawing to photorealistic space is the whole pitch.
tasks.stretch: Add a 15-second walkthrough video from the same model and one AI-generated render variation (AI Render or ZSky AI), then note what the AI got wrong that your to-scale model got right. Directing AI and correcting it is the premium skill.

tasks.title: Turn a Weak Product Listing Into a Buyable One
tasks.proves: You can take a flat, ignored product listing and rebuild it into one that ranks and converts: one of the most-requested e-commerce VA skills.

prerequisites.skill: Listing anatomy (title, bullets, description, images, A+ content)
prerequisites.why: You can't fix a listing if you don't know which part does which job. The title ranks; the bullets sell; the images close.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: Amazon Seller University (open) has a free walkthrough of every listing element in under an hour.

prerequisites.skill: Basic keyword research
prerequisites.why: A listing rewrite that isn't driven by what buyers actually search is just prettier guessing.
prerequisites.ifYouDont: Helium 10's free tier lets you pull real search terms for any product; their free tutorials show how.

resources.name: A real public product listing
resources.what: Pick any live Amazon or Shopify product with an obviously weak listing to stand in for your 'client's' store: real data, no invented product.

resources.name: Helium 10
resources.what: Free tier for keyword research and a listing-quality audit.

resources.name: ChatGPT
resources.what: Free tier to draft and tighten copy fast: you direct it, you don't trust it blind.

brief.scenario: A seller's product is buried on page five. The listing has a vague title, three lazy bullets, one dark photo, and no A+ content. Sales are flat and they blame the market. It's not the market; it's the listing. Rebuild it.
brief.deliverable: A rewritten listing: a keyword-driven title, five benefit-led bullets, a scannable description, an image/A+ shot list, and the keyword list you built it on, presented next to the original.
constraints: Keyword-driven, not keyword-stuffed. Every term must read like a human wrote it.
No invented claims, fake reviews, or made-up specs. Honest copy is the only kind that survives a return rate.
Every bullet must lead with a buyer benefit, not a feature spec.
steps: Pick one real, weak public listing and screenshot the original as your 'before'.
Pull the top search terms buyers actually use for that product (Helium 10 free tier).
Rewrite the title and five bullets around those terms: benefit first, keyword woven in.
Draft a scannable description and a shot list for the images and A+ content.
Lay your version beside the original and write two lines on why each change lifts rank or conversion.

definitionOfDone: The new title leads with the product's top real search term and reads naturally.
All five bullets lead with a benefit, not a spec.
The keyword list you used is attached, not just implied.
Before and after sit side by side so the improvement is obvious at a glance.
selfCritique: Would a buyer scanning for three seconds understand what this is and why it's better?
Did I write for the search algorithm and the human, or stuff keywords and hope?
Is there a single claim here I couldn't back up if the product arrived tomorrow?
tasks.presentIt: Present it as a rank-and-conversion play: 'Original listing → page five, flat sales; rebuilt listing → keyword-led, benefit-first, A+ mapped.' Put both versions side by side: the contrast is the proof you can do this for a real store.
tasks.stretch: Do the same teardown for two competitor listings in the same category and write a one-page 'why theirs wins or loses' note. A VA who can read a whole category, not just one listing, is a strategist a seller keeps.
